andrew-holman-1905-08-28.A1:
Timely Interference Prevented F.
L. Townsend From Hanging
Alleged Negro Thief.
HAD ROPE AROUND HIS NECK
Witnesses Say Mrs. Townsend, Clad in Nightgown, Applauded Her Spouse's Wild Performance After Helping Him to Tie Prisoner's Hands and Fect.
Bloodcurdling yells and cries breaking the stillness of the crisp night air attracted a number of people to 233 Thirty-third street, the home and grocery store of Frank L. Townsend, last night shortly after 10 o'clock.

Tracing the sounds to the small yard in the rear of the house, half a dozen men who had run from Washington avenue and from the Eagles' home, corner Huntington avenue and Thirty-third street, came upon a strange scene. On the ground lay a negro, bound hand and foot and gasping for breath between yells and cries for help. Seated upon the prostrate body were three white figures—two women and a man, all clad in night gowns and in their bare feet.

Engaged in tying a half-inch rope around the negro's neck was another white figure—Mr. Townsend, also bare footed and wearing a nightshirt.

At first the sight was ludicrous and the astonished spectators were inclined to laugh, but when they saw what was about to happen the laughs died in their throats.

When the rope was securely fastened about the prisoner's throat, the three who had been sitting upon the man rose and, according to eye-witnesses, Townsend threw the rope over a beam and prepared to play the part of Judge Lynch. One of the women, who proved to be Townsend's daughter, then fled into the house, but, according to the story, the other, Mrs. Townsend, seated herself upon a box and, in spite of her scant attire and the chilly atmosphere, began to watch the proceedings with apparent calm.

Several of the spectators interfered at this juncture, calling upon Townsend to desist. From the windows of an adjoining house cries of "Don't kill that man!" The witnesses declared that Mrs. Townsend, still seated upon the box with her bare limbs crossed, called, "Go ahead and hang him. I never saw a nigger hung in my life."

Fortunately, the protests of the spectators had their effect and, beyond hammering the negro about in the dir- and batting him over the head with a club, Mr. Townsend did nothing rash, so the witnesses say.

After some minutes had passed, during which time the spectators learned that the negro had attempted to break into the lunch wagon, which Townsend drives to the shipyard every day. Some one was sent to a telephone and the patrol wagon was summoned.

In due time the wagon arrived with Driver Pelham Smith and Patrelman Woodward aboard. The officers relieved Townsend of his prisoner and, after some time had been spent in untying the ropes which were bound around the negro's arms, body and legs, that much battered "coon" was placed in the wagon and taken to the station.

andrew-holman-1905-08-28.A2:
BOTH ARE OLD OFFENDERS.
Sam Barksdale, Pal of Andrew Holbrook, Arrested Yesterday.
Officer Padgett yesterday arrested Sam Barksdale, the negro who was with Andrew Holbrook, also colored, when the latter was caught in the act of breaking into Frank L. Townsend's lunch wagon, at 233 Thirty-third street, Monday night. Holbrook "blew on his pal" and the officers easily located Barksdale.

Chief Reynolds believes that both men are wanted in Danville on the charge of house breaking and if it is found that the act of breaking into the lunch wagon does not constitute house breaking, the pair probably will be turned over to the Danville authorities for trial.

Holbrook was sent to the penitentiary for a term of four years several years ago for shooting Barksdale. Barksdale is also said to have been to the penitentiary. Holbrook looked very much the worse for wear when he appeared in the police court yesterday and on his neck was plainly to be seen the mark left by the rope with which Townsend is said to have been preparing to hang him when spectators interfered.

WAS ABOUT TO HANG
NEGRO WHEN HELP CAME
Summary Action of Grocer, Whose Lunch Wagon Was Robbed.
(Special to The Times-Dispatch.)
NEWPORT NEWS VA. August 29-

(Special to The Times-Dispatch.)

NEWPORT NEWS, VA., August 29. Andrew Holbrook, a negro, who attempted to break into a movable lunch wagon belonging to F. L. Townsend, a grocer, narrowly escaped death at the hands of the grocer. Townsend had put a rope about the negro's neck and was about to string him up, when persons who had been attracted to the scene by the negro's cries interfered.

To-day it developed that Holbrook is wanted in Danville on the charge of housebreaking. S. L. Barksdale, another negro, who was with Holbrook at the time of the attempted robbery, was arrested to-day, and it is believed that he, too, is wanted in Danville. Both men have served terms in the penitentiary.

WHITE MEN CHARGED
WITH WHITEECAPPING
Negro Swears Out Warrants On the Advice of Other White Residents of Lake Park, Ga.
Valdosta, G.a, August 9.—Warrants were sworn out this morning for several prominent citizens of Lake Park, charging them with whitecapping Bill Pierce a negro of that place.

The warrants charge them with assault with intent to murder, and are sworn out by the negro himself, but under the advice of white citizens. The men named in the warrant are Justice of the Peace Joseph T. Corbett, R. W. Wheeler, Saul Carter and Henry Connell. Several days ago the negro was ordered to leave the community at once, the object being to get rid of his testimony in a whisky-selling case.

He consulted other citizens, and they advised him not to leave. Night before last a party of men went to his house and took him him out and gave him a drubbing, leaving the man about half half dead. Deputy Sheriff Crosby went to Lake Park this morning to serve the warrants.

Negro Shot on Train.
At a late hour last night, Deputy Sheriff J. P. Brentz shot and killed a negro whose name is supposed to be John Hill. The shooting took place in a Southeren Railway passenger train in the western part of the county near Coalburg. The negro was boisterous on the train and picking a quarrel with other negro passengers when the conductor informed Deputy Sheriff Brentz, who happened to be going to Republic. The deputy approached the negro, when he offered resistance. The negro placed his hand to the rear pocket as if to draw a gun. He took his hand away on seeing the officer show a pistol. When the officer had replaced his own weapon the negro made another move to his pocket when Deputy Sheriff Brentz pulled his gun rapidly and fired two shots at the negro, killing him almost instantly.
john-hill-coalburg-1905-08-15.A2:
NEGRO MAN KILLED BY DEPUTY BRENTS
ATTEMPTED TO DRAW WEAPON WHILE UNDER ARREST ON SOUTHERN PASSENGER TRAIN MONDAY NIGHT.
Information reached the sheriff's office yesterday morning to the effect that Deputy Sheriff J. P. Brents had shot and killed a negro by the named of Hill on a Southern passenger train between Birmingham and Republic Monday night about 11 o'clock.

From the statement made by Deputy Brents and eye witnesses to the shooting, the conductor had asked Brents to go into the negro car and arrest a boisterous negro. The conductor warned the deputy of the dangerous character of the negro.

Deputy Brents then went into the car and ordered the man to throw up his hands, which he promptly did. Later, however, he made an effort to put his hand in his hip pocket. Drawing his pistol from his scabbard, the deputy demanded that the negro again throw up his hands. He did not do so, but instead made another effort to draw a weapon, and upon a second command the officer fired twice on the negro with a .45 calibre Colts revolver. The negro was killed instantly.

The shooting is being carefully investigated, but from the information they have received so far, the officers believe the killing was in self-defense.

MOB CONDUCTS DOUBLE LYNCH

Two Negroes at Gloria, Tex., Escape After Case Is Heard by "Kang and Other Functionaries Selected Man Who Counseled Moderation Defense—Jury of Twelve Men

DEPUTIES CARRY OUT SENTENCE

REPUBLIC SPECIAL.

Houston, Tex., Aug. 20—A mob of 200 men quietly formed at Gloria to-day and captured Si Liddell, a negro who had made improper remarks to a young white woman, and another negro, Jones, and hurried them to a pasture where there were several trees. Ropes were placed around the negroes' necks and all preparations were made for a double lynching.

Cooler heads in the party made talks, counseling moderation. It was at length decided that the negroes should be tried.

A tribunal was organized with judge and sheriff, and later a jury of twelve men was selected.

ATTORNEY FOR NEGROES.

One man, who had warned the mob to go slow, was named as attorney for the two defendants, and another was chosen for prosecuting attorney.

The trial was under a clump of trees and continued an hour. Many witnesses were put on the stand, and those who had no direct testimony testified as to the character of the accused negroes.

The fury at length retired and a verdict of guilt was returned five minutes later. The punishment was not fixed at death, but at whipping. The verdict gave Liddell 100 lashes and Jones twenty-five. The sheriff denounced ten of the leaders of the mob to assist him in carrying out the verdict.

DEPUTIES ADMINISTER LASHES. Liddell was tied to a tree with his back bared, and each of the deputies cealt him ten lashes with ropes and straps. Jones received his quota in the same manner.

The negroes were badly used up, but were able to get away when released. They were warned to depart, and by midnight they were believed to be far away from the town.

The dummy court was managed with as much decorum as a regular tribunal, and the judge at one state of the trial imposed a fine of £5 on a witness for contempt and forced payment on the spot.

There were several negroes among the mob's members, and they took an active part in the trial.
si-liddell-glory-1905-08-19.A3:
Negroes Whipped.
Two young negro men were arrested Saturday morning near Glory, twenty miles west of Clarksville, Texas, charged with making defamatory remarks about the daughter of a prominent white farmer. They were kept chained during the day in a building and Saturday night were carried out in a meadow, half a mile east of the village, where a crowd of 700 residents of the community had assembled, composed equally of blacks and whites. A committee of ten, composed of five whites and five blacks, was appointed to try the culprits. Several witnesses were examined and the prisoners were found guilty of having uttered the slanderous remarks. One of them was sentenced to receive forty lashes, while the other was sentenced to receive twenty-five lashes. The whipping was administered by the negro members of the committee, each of the five giving the culprit who who had been sentenced to forty lashes, eight lashes, and the one who had been sentenced to twenty-five lashes, five. After the whipping the men were turned loose and were given five days to leave the community.
si-liddell-glory-1905-08-19.A4:
SLANDERERS LASHED They Were Negroes, But Negroes Help to Punish Them.
Clarksville, Tex., Aug. 21.—Two young negroes were arrested yesterday morning near Glory, 20 miles east of here, charged with making defamatory remarks about the daughter of a prominent white farmer. They were kept chained during the day in a building and Saturday night were carried out in a meadow half a mile east of the village, where a crowd of 700 residents of the community, blacks and whites, had assembled. A committee of 10, composed of five white and five black citizens, were appointed to try the culprits. Several witnesses were examined and the prisoners were found guilty of having uttered the slanders. One of them was sentenced to receive 40 lashes, the other 25. The whipping was administered by the negro members of the committee. After the whipping the culprits were turned loose and were told to leave the community in five days.
si-liddell-glory-1905-08-19.A8: A mob which was about to hang a negro in Texas concluded to give him a trial, with the result that he was found deserving of nothing more than a lashing. This is something which might be commended to other anti-negro mobs, and which might be found more productive of desired results.
